arml-2016-power-01b.title: Move parallel to an axis
arml-2016-power-01b.body:
Euclidean and taxi-distance agree exactly when the displacement is horizontal or vertical. Moving 5 units from $(3,2)$ along an axis gives $(8,2)$, $(-2,2)$, $(3,7)$ or $(3,-3)$; any one of these works.

**Answer: e.g. $(8,2)$**

arml-2016-power-01c.title: Use a 3-4-5 triangle
arml-2016-power-01c.body:
A displacement $(\pm3,\pm4)$ or $(\pm4,\pm3)$ has Euclidean length $5$ and taxi-length $3+4=7$. So e.g. $(3+3,2+4)=(6,6)$ works (as do the other seven sign/order choices).

**Answer: e.g. $(6,6)$**

arml-2016-power-02b.title: Example
arml-2016-power-02b.body:
$P=(2,4)$: $d_T(A,P)=2+0=2$ and $d_T(P,B)=2+4=6$, total $8=d_T(A,B)$, and $2+4\ne4$. (By part c, every point of the square $[0,4]\times[0,4]$ works.)

**Answer: e.g. $(2,4)$**

arml-2016-power-02c.title: Triangle inequality on each coordinate
arml-2016-power-02c.body:
For $P=(x,y)$:
$$d_T(A,P)+d_T(P,B)=\big(|x|+|4-x|\big)+\big(|4-y|+|y|\big)\ge x+(4-x)+(4-y)+y=8=d_T(A,B),$$
using $|r|\ge r$, with equality iff $x\ge0$, $4-x\ge0$, $4-y\ge0$, $y\ge0$. So the set is the square $0\le x\le4$, $0\le y\le4$ (boundary included). ∎

arml-2016-power-02c.title: Case analysis
arml-2016-power-02c.body: Inside the square ($0\le x,y\le4$) the sum is $x+(4-y)+(4-x)+y=8$. If, say, $x<0$ and $0\le y\le4$, the sum is $(-x)+(4-y)+(4-x)+y=8-2x>8$; similarly for $x>4$, $y<0$, $y>4$ (each out-of-range coordinate adds twice its excess). So exactly the square works. ∎

arml-2016-power-03a.title: Differences are preserved
arml-2016-power-03a.body: For $A=(x_1,y_1)$, $B=(x_2,y_2)$: $d_T(A',B')=|(x_2+h)-(x_1+h)|+|(y_2+k)-(y_1+k)|=|x_2-x_1|+|y_2-y_1|=d_T(A,B)$. The same holds for the other two sides, so yes. ∎

arml-2016-power-03b.title: Compute the image
arml-2016-power-03b.body: The reflection sends $(x,y)\mapsto(x,2k-y)$. Then $d_T(A',B')=|x_2-x_1|+|(2k-y_2)-(2k-y_1)|=|x_2-x_1|+|y_1-y_2|=d_T(A,B)$, and likewise for the other sides. So yes. ∎

arml-2016-power-03c.title: Compare one side
arml-2016-power-03c.body: $O'=(0,0)$, $R'=(4\sqrt2,4\sqrt2)$, $D'=(-2\sqrt2,2\sqrt2)$. The taxi side lengths of $\triangle ORD$ are $4,8,12$, but $d_T(O',R')=8\sqrt2$, which is none of these. So the triangles are not taxi-congruent. ∎

arml-2016-power-04a.title: Double angle
arml-2016-power-04a.body:
Let $\theta$ be the angle of ray $OA$ with the positive $x$-axis: $\tan\theta=\frac12$. Ray $OB$ makes angle $2\theta$, and $\tan2\theta=\frac{2\cdot\frac12}{1-\frac14}=\frac43$. So $B$ lies on $y=\frac43x$, and with $\gcd(m,n)=1$, $(m,n)=(3,4)$.

**Answer: $(3,4)$**

arml-2016-power-04a.title: Reflect P across line OA
arml-2016-power-04a.body:
$\angle BOA=\angle AOP$ means ray $OB$ is the reflection of ray $OP$ across line $OA$ (direction $(2,1)/\sqrt5$). Reflecting $(1,0)$: $2\,\frac{(1,0)\cdot(2,1)}{5}(2,1)-(1,0)=\frac45(2,1)-(1,0)=\left(\frac35,\frac45\right)$. So $(m,n)=(3,4)$.

**Answer: $(3,4)$**

arml-2016-power-04b.title: Find the intersection points
arml-2016-power-04b.body:
Ray $OA$ ($y=\frac x2$) meets $x+y=1$ at $\left(\frac23,\frac13\right)$; ray $OB$ ($y=\frac43x$) meets it at $\left(\frac37,\frac47\right)$; ray $OP$ meets it at $(1,0)$.

- $\angle AOP$: $d_T\!\left((1,0),(\frac23,\frac13)\right)=\frac13+\frac13=\frac23$.
- $\angle BOA$: $d_T\!\left((\frac23,\frac13),(\frac37,\frac47)\right)=\frac5{21}+\frac5{21}=\frac{10}{21}$.

So congruent Euclidean angles intercept arcs of different taxi-lengths on the unit taxi-circle.

**Answer: $\frac23$ (for $\angle AOP$) and $\frac{10}{21}$ (for $\angle BOA$)**

arml-2016-power-05a.title: Definition
arml-2016-power-05a.body:
The taxi-circle is $\{(x,y): |x|+|y|=17\}$: the square with vertices $(\pm17,0)$ and $(0,\pm17)$, whose sides lie on $\pm x\pm y=17$.

**Answer: $|x|+|y|=17$**

arml-2016-power-05b.title: Measure the semicircle
arml-2016-power-05b.body:
The semicircle from $(17,0)$ through $(0,17)$ to $(-17,0)$ consists of two sides, each of taxi-length $d_T((17,0),(0,17))=34$. So the semi-circumference is $68$, and $\pi_T=\frac{68}{17}=4$.

**Answer: 4**

arml-2016-power-05c.title: General radius
arml-2016-power-05c.body: The taxi-circle of radius $r$ is $|x|+|y|=r$. A semicircle from $(r,0)$ through $(0,r)$ to $(-r,0)$ has taxi-length $d_T((r,0),(0,r))+d_T((0,r),(-r,0))=2r+2r=4r$, so $\pi_T=\frac{4r}{r}=4$, independent of $r$. ∎

arml-2016-power-05d.title: Arc length over radius
arml-2016-power-05d.body:
$d_T(O,C)=d_T(O,B)=4$, so both lie on the taxi-circle $|x|+|y|=4$. The arc from $C$ to $B$ passes through $(0,4)$: $d_T((3,1),(0,4))+d_T((0,4),(-1,3))=6+2=8$. So $m_T\angle COB=\frac84=2$ taxi-radians.

**Answer: 2**

arml-2016-power-06a.title: Slide along the taxi-circle
arml-2016-power-06a.body:
$O'=O$. In the first quadrant, moving from $(x,y)$ to $(x-t,y+t)$ stays on the same taxi-circle and covers taxi-arc length $2t$.

- $A$: radius $8$, arc length $8\cdot1=8$, so $t=4$: $A'=(4,4)$.
- $R$: radius $4$, arc length $4$, so $t=2$: $R'=(1,3)$.

**Answer: $O'=(0,0)$, $A'=(4,4)$, $R'=(1,3)$**

arml-2016-power-06b.title: Compare the third side
arml-2016-power-06b.body: The rotation gives $A'=(4,4)$, $R'=(1,3)$ (see part a). The sides from $O$ are preserved by construction, but $d_T(A,R)=|3-8|+|1-0|=6$ while $d_T(A',R')=|1-4|+|3-4|=4$. So the triangles are not taxi-congruent. ∎

arml-2016-power-07a.title: Example
arml-2016-power-07a.body: Take $C=(-1,1)$, $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,1)$. Then $d_T(C,A)=2=d_T(M,O)$ and $d_T(A,B)=2=d_T(O,D)$. On the taxi-circle $|x|+|y|=2$, the arc from $B$ to $C$ (through $(0,2)$) has length $2+2=4$, so $m_T\angle CAB=\frac42=2$; similarly the arc from $D=(2,0)$ to $M=(0,2)$ has length $4$, so $m_T\angle MOD=2$. But $d_T(C,B)=2$ while $d_T(M,D)=4$, so the triangles are not congruent. ∎

arml-2016-power-07b.title: Example
arml-2016-power-07b.body:
Take $P=(-1,1)$, $I=(0,0)$, $G=(2,0)$. Then $d_T(P,I)=2$, $d_T(I,G)=2$, $d_T(P,G)=3+1=4$, matching $d_T(M,O)=2$, $d_T(O,D)=2$, $d_T(M,D)=4$.

Angles: on $|x|+|y|=2$, the arc from $G=(2,0)$ to $P=(-1,1)$ through $(0,2)$ has length $4+2=6$, so $m_T\angle PIG=3$, whereas $m_T\angle MOD=\frac42=2$. So the triangles are not congruent. ∎

arml-2016-power-08b.title: Drop a perpendicular
arml-2016-power-08b.body:
Since $OA$ is horizontal, $d_E(O,A)=d_T(O,A)$, so $\cos_T\angle AOB=\dfrac{d_E(O,B)}{d_T(O,B)}\cos\angle AOB$.

Let $B'$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to line $OA$ (a horizontal line). Then $OB'$ is horizontal and $B'B$ vertical, so $d_T(O,B)=d_E(O,B')+d_E(B',B)=d_E(O,B)\big(|\cos\angle AOB|+|\sin\angle AOB|\big)$. Substituting,
$$\cos_T\angle AOB=\frac{\cos\angle AOB}{|\cos\angle AOB|+|\sin\angle AOB|}.\ ∎$$

arml-2016-power-08c.title: Taxi-length via the horizontal
arml-2016-power-08c.body:
Let $A'$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to line $PQ$ (horizontal). Then $QA'$ is horizontal and $A'A$ vertical, so
$$d_T(Q,A)=d_E(Q,A')+d_E(A',A)=d_E(Q,A)\big(|\cos\angle AQP|+|\sin\angle AQP|\big).$$
Similarly $d_T(Q,B)=d_E(Q,B)\big(|\cos\angle BQP|+|\sin\angle BQP|\big)$. Substituting these into
$\cos_T\angle AQB=\dfrac{d_E(Q,A)d_E(Q,B)}{d_T(Q,A)d_T(Q,B)}\cos\angle AQB$ gives the formula. ∎

arml-2016-power-09a.title: Decompose into horizontal and vertical legs
arml-2016-power-09a.body:
Let $p=d_T(A,C')=d_E(A,C')$ and $q=d_T(B,C')=d_E(B,C')$ (horizontal segments), so $c_T=p+q$, $b_T=p+h_T$, $a_T=q+h_T$ (each of $AC$, $BC$ splits into a horizontal and a vertical leg). With Euclidean lengths $b=d_E(A,C)$, $a=d_E(B,C)$, $c=d_E(A,B)=c_T$, we have $p=b\cos A$, $q=a\cos B$, $h_T=b\sin A=a\sin B$.

By definition, $b_T\cos_TA=b_T\cdot\dfrac{b\,c}{b_T\,c_T}\cos A=b\cos A=p$ (using $c=c_T$). Therefore
$$b_T+c_T-2b_T\cos_TA=(p+h_T)+(p+q)-2p=q+h_T=a_T.\ ∎$$

arml-2016-power-09b.title: Same decomposition
arml-2016-power-09b.body:
Let $p=d_T(A,C')=d_E(A,C')$ and $q=d_T(B,C')=d_E(B,C')$ (horizontal segments), so $c_T=p+q$, $b_T=p+h_T$, $a_T=q+h_T$ (each of $AC$, $BC$ splits into a horizontal and a vertical leg). With Euclidean lengths $b=d_E(A,C)$, $a=d_E(B,C)$, $c=d_E(A,B)=c_T$, we have $p=b\cos A$, $q=a\cos B$, $h_T=b\sin A=a\sin B$.

$a_T\cos_TB=a_T\cdot\dfrac{a\,c}{a_T\,c_T}\cos B=a\cos B=q$. So
$$a_T+c_T-2a_T\cos_TB=(q+h_T)+(p+q)-2q=p+h_T=b_T.\ ∎$$

arml-2016-power-09c.title: Use cos C = −cos(A+B)
arml-2016-power-09c.body:
Let $p=d_T(A,C')=d_E(A,C')$ and $q=d_T(B,C')=d_E(B,C')$ (horizontal segments), so $c_T=p+q$, $b_T=p+h_T$, $a_T=q+h_T$ (each of $AC$, $BC$ splits into a horizontal and a vertical leg). With Euclidean lengths $b=d_E(A,C)$, $a=d_E(B,C)$, $c=d_E(A,B)=c_T$, we have $p=b\cos A$, $q=a\cos B$, $h_T=b\sin A=a\sin B$.

Since $C=\pi-A-B$, $\cos C=\sin A\sin B-\cos A\cos B$. Then
$$a_Tb_T\cos_TC=ab\cos C=(b\sin A)(a\sin B)-(b\cos A)(a\cos B)=h_T^2-pq.$$
With $p=b_T-h_T$ and $q=a_T-h_T$: $h_T^2-pq=h_T^2-(b_T-h_T)(a_T-h_T)=(a_T+b_T)h_T-a_Tb_T$. Hence
$$a_T^2+b_T^2-2a_Tb_T\cos_TC=a_T^2+b_T^2+2a_Tb_T-2(a_T+b_T)h_T=(a_T+b_T)(a_T+b_T-2h_T).$$
Finally $a_T+b_T-2h_T=p+q=c_T$, so dividing by $a_T+b_T$ gives the result. ∎

arml-2016-power-10.title: Reduce to the Euclidean Law of Sines
arml-2016-power-10.body:
Let $a,b,c$ be the Euclidean side lengths. By definition $\sin_TC=\dfrac{ab}{a_Tb_T}\sin C$, so
$$\frac{c_T}{\sin_TC}=\frac{a_Tb_Tc_T}{abc}\cdot\frac{c}{\sin C}.$$
Likewise $\dfrac{a_T}{\sin_TA}=\dfrac{a_Tb_Tc_T}{abc}\cdot\dfrac{a}{\sin A}$ and $\dfrac{b_T}{\sin_TB}=\dfrac{a_Tb_Tc_T}{abc}\cdot\dfrac{b}{\sin B}$. By the Euclidean Law of Sines $\frac a{\sin A}=\frac b{\sin B}=\frac c{\sin C}$, so the three taxi ratios are equal. ∎

arml-2016-power-10.title: Area
arml-2016-power-10.body:
From the definition, $d_T(C,A)\,d_T(C,B)\sin_T\angle ACB=d_E(C,A)\,d_E(C,B)\sin\angle ACB=2[ABC]$. Applying this at each vertex:
$$b_Tc_T\sin_TA=a_Tc_T\sin_TB=a_Tb_T\sin_TC=2[ABC].$$
Dividing by $a_Tb_Tc_T$ and taking reciprocals gives $\frac{a_T}{\sin_TA}=\frac{b_T}{\sin_TB}=\frac{c_T}{\sin_TC}$. ∎
